Union graph with Panama Papers: 838,293 nodes and 1,286,362 edges. Scores are relative to the loaded graph — compare them within one graph, not across graphs.

The leak is huge. The trail is human-sized.

The ICIJ Offshore Leaks database is millions of records across companies, officers, intermediaries and addresses. The relationships are the story — but the public CSVs are not a graph. Tracing a chain by hand means opening record after record, deciding which shared address matters, and remembering every step.

Scale

3.3 million relationship rows

The public relationship file has 3.3 million rows; the CSVs total roughly 600 MB. There is no join key you can eyeball.

Ambiguity

The same name is not the same record

Names repeat, IDs collide across files, and some links are soft matches. A guess is not evidence.

Hubs

Some links are everywhere

In the union graph, a single address has 37,338 core neighbours. High degree makes a link less informative, not more.

A shared address can be a real lead or a clearing-house hub. The graph has to tell the difference.

Ask in plain language. Get a path you can inspect.

The question is simple: how is A connected to B? The answer is a traversal — not a search result — with the score, the records and the excluded hubs attached.

Ask

No Cypher required

Ask “What is the strongest recorded connection between X and Y?” The agent chooses the right graph tool for the question.

Rank

Paths, strongest first

Hub-respecting paths come back ranked by connection relevance, each with the intermediate nodes and degrees that produced the score.

Explore

Click through the graph

Select a node, expand its neighbours, click an edge. The raw link text, role, dates and source record are one click away.

Verify

Evidence behind every claim

Every answer carries its path, relationship types, source records, node degrees, limitations and any excluded hubs that changed the result.

The score is the mean rarity of the two intermediate nodes. It says the recorded link is rare and specific in this graph — not that anything is wrong. On the union graph the same path scores 10.45 because the score is relative to the live node count.

The graph does the work.

The LLM does exactly two things: pick a tool, and turn structured results into a plain-language explanation. Pathfinding, hub filtering and scoring are Cypher plus Python — deterministic, auditable and cacheable.

Data flows from the public ICIJ CSVs into a prepared slice, then into FalkorDB. Four fixed graph tools sit behind a read-only MCP server. The agent decides which tool to call; the grounding layer checks the answer before the API returns it.

The “strongest connection” query is an exact-depth path search with a hub predicate on every intermediate hop, ranked by the mean rarity of those hops. A post-hoc Python filter over unfiltered paths timed out at 60 s next to a 36k-degree hub; pruning inside the traversal returns in milliseconds.

“If removing FalkorDB leaves a feature working, that feature is wrong.”The design test used for every feature

Public ICIJ CSVs → prepare_slice.py → graph

  1. FalkorDB graph

    One node per record, with degree_core stored at import. Cypher does the path search, the in-traversal hub pruning and the degree scoring.

    278,693 nodes · 562,700 edges · offshore

  2. Read-only MCP server

    Four fixed, size-capped tools: search_entity, strongest_connection, shared_neighbors, get_neighbors. No write tools.

  3. LangGraph agent

    The model picks a tool, reads the structured result, repeats. It does not write Cypher, and every loop is capped.

  4. Grounding layer

    Every ID, quoted name, degree and country code is checked against the tool results. A violation is replaced by a deterministic fallback.

  5. FastAPI + web UI

    /ask and /connect return the answer envelope; the UI renders ranked paths, node degrees and edge records with Cytoscape.js.

Same tools, second client

The MCP server was tested from an external opencode client in an empty folder. It made two search calls and one strongest_connection call and returned the correct 3-hop / 9.35 answer in about 20 seconds.

Four choices that make the answer defensible.

The product is not “an LLM over a CSV.” The graph, the score and the grounding each do a job that cannot be replaced by a prompt.

Score

Rarity, not volume.

A link through a hub is weak evidence: in the union graph, one address has 37,338 core neighbours. A rarely used officer is a more specific connection. Each intermediate node contributes a log-rarity weight.

score(path) = mean over intermediate nodes m of
  ln( (N + 1) / (degree_core(m) + 1) )

N = number of nodes in the loaded graph

Mean, not sum — padding a path cannot raise the score. Endpoints contribute nothing. A direct link has no intermediate nodes, so its score is “not applicable”.

Identity

Possible match is a label, not a shortcut.

similar · possible match

Soft edges (similar, same_as, underlying) stay separate types, are drawn dashed, and always carry a possible-match note. The agent must say “possible match” — never “same company”.

1,139 IDs appear in both the officer and intermediary files with identical names and country codes. They are stored as one node with both labels, because splitting them would delete real connectivity.

Grounding

The model does not get the last word.

  • IDs, quoted names, degrees and country codes are checked against tool output.
  • Identity claims are downgraded when only soft edges link the records.
  • A violation is replaced from evidence — never returned silently.

The grounding step is code, not another LLM call. It is the reason a sentence in the UI can be traced back to a node or an edge record.

MCP

One server, more than one agent.

# external opencode client, empty folder
offshore_search_entity_tool {"name": "GALAXY ASIA LIMITED."}
offshore_search_entity_tool {"name": "TO.CE.CO LIMITED."}
offshore_strongest_connection_tool {"source_id": "123345", "target_id": "170362"}
→ 3 hops · 9.35 (offshore) · ~20 s

The MCP layer is a real interface, not a private function: another model discovered the tools and answered the flagship question from the same read-only server.

Five things the graph taught me.

Short lessons from the decisions log — each one changed the code, not just the README.

  1. Let the data settle the schema.

    1,139 IDs appear in both the officer and intermediary files with identical names and country codes. Two pretty nodes would have deleted real connectivity, so each ID is one node with both labels — and the choice is documented.

  2. Put the hub filter inside the traversal.

    A post-hoc filter over unfiltered paths timed out at 60 seconds next to a 36k-degree hub. A per-hop predicate in the Cypher pattern returns in milliseconds. The filter belongs in the query shape, not in a cleanup step.

  3. A score is only honest if it says what it is not.

    The rarity score measures how informative a recorded link is. It is not a probability of wrongdoing or kinship. Endpoints contribute nothing, the mean prevents padding, and a direct link has no score at all.

  4. Ambiguity needs a UI, not a guess.

    When a name resolves to more than one exact record, the agent returns the candidates as buttons. A pinned node ID goes straight to the path tools and is never silently replaced by a fuzzy match.

  5. Grounding must be code, not vibes.

    Every ID, name, degree and country code in an answer is checked against tool output. A soft-edge identity claim is downgraded to “possible match”, and a violation triggers a deterministic fallback instead of a confident sentence.

Documented limits, not hidden

  • No verified shared-structure (officer + address + intermediary) demo pair has been found yet.
  • No deep Panama-only path pair yet; depth 6 is not safe on hub-blocked pairs, while depth 5 is.
  • Scores are relative to the loaded graph. Compare within one graph, not across graphs.

Small stack. The graph is the point.

One local Docker service, one Python backend, one MCP server and a zero-dependency web UI. The only frontend library is a vendored copy of Cytoscape.js, so the demo works offline.

Offshore Investigator

An independent demonstration built for Graph Hacks: Context for AI Agents (WeMakeDevs × FalkorDB), Track 01, 15–18 October 2026.

Data © ICIJ and contributors. Code MIT licensed. Appearing in this public data implies no wrongdoing.

Data & license

The data is the public ICIJ Offshore Leaks Database, with Panama Papers included in the union graph. It keeps its own license and terms; the MIT license covers the code in this repository only, not the data.

Raw CSVs are never committed to the repository. The app is read-only over a local prepared slice.

AI & neutrality

Built with AI assistance: opencode as the coding agent and Claude for planning and prompt writing, disclosed in the AI usage log. Every query and design choice was reviewed by the author.

A connection relevance score is not a probability of wrongdoing or kinship. Soft edges are possible matches, never confirmed identities.
